pairs.old: Fishery catches over 56 years give each year's share of sockeye salmon coming home to the Fraser River north or south of Vancouver Island, and that share goes with a physics model's reading of Earth's magnetic field, how close its reading at points along each way comes to its reading at the Fraser's mouth in the year of those salmon going out to sea as young fish; magnetic imprinting is its authors' explaining of that going-with, and no observing in it is a salmon observing magnetism. Close to its river a salmon likely finds its own stream by smell, and a 1953 test finds all but 8 of 73 salmon with their noses open coming back up the branch of their first capture, and 28 of 70 with a plug in their noses going up the other branch. A salmon's going home is its own parities with its surface, from its own side, its home its own prior same-existing now-existing in it; the model's reading going with it from outside, 2.4, imprinting and long-term memory a field's story of a store over it, and what a salmon's surface is from its own side across an ocean is still-possibling. Along a river a salmon goes from each is-not, not that water, to is.

In laboratory corridors 3.0 and 3.6 m wide, people, mostly students, walk in two opposite streams over 22 trials, up to 350 people walking in the experiments as a whole: in some trials stable lanes form at once and on their own, and in others lanes form and go on shifting. Its authors give a lane as forming with a person going close behind someone going the same way, fewer clashes with the stream going the other way its aim. A lane patterns along, each walker co-chaining behind another from its own side, and betweens across with the stream going the other way, the lanes uncovering between the walkers.

Workers of Coptotermes gestroi in a laboratory arena collect clay fairly evenly over a disk and put it down at the tips of pillars, at the top edges and side tips of walls and at the disk's edge; a model growing by a surface's curving alone gives the building's shapes, not its pace, and each place of putting down is a place of evaporating most, its authors proposing that a termite senses curving through evaporating; with its pellets heating at 100 °C for an hour to clear any chemical marking, the building goes on all the same, its authors not ruling out a pheromone's part. Grassé's stigmergy names a building going with signals in the structure itself, each termite's putting down going with what putting down already shapes, its own and others'. A building patterns along its own surface, each termite co-chaining along a curving already showing, from its own side, and the building is in no termite alone.

pairs.old: A mother and her fetus are a same-existing-society of two at a placenta: the fetus's trophoblast cells show HLA-C to the mother's KIR receptors, which goes with how far the mother's spiral arteries remodel into the placenta's blood supply, the layer between them forms from cells fusing by the mammal's own syncytin genes, and cells may pass between them, male cells, likely a son's from a pregnancy, going on in some women's brains for several decades.

Two crews join through rock by each other's sharing. The Siloam inscription, from Hezekiah's tunnel in Jerusalem, gives an account of quarrymen digging toward each other from two ends, with three cubits still to cut a man's voice calling to his fellow through a fissure or overlap in the rock, axe striking axe as they break through, and water then going from the spring to the pool for 1,200 cubits, the rock 100 cubits over the stonecutters' heads. The tunnel of Eupalinos on Samos, of the sixth century BC, 1,036 m long, goes from two ends toward a joining under a hill over 200 m high, its two straight shafts each aiming toward that joining and a zigzag close to it: one reading is a turn by design, each shaft turning and the two crossing; some scholars read the tunnel's winding as errors and their correcting; and others read each crew as likely hearing the other's hammering through the rock and turning with it; its vertical offset at the joining given as 4 cm by Hermann Kienast and as 60 cm elsewhere. Each crew goes on from its own side, and a voice or a hammering through the rock, a surface opening between the two crews across, orients the last cubits: co-competencing, a fixing between the crews loosening two-way, the tunnel of rock its artifact and its joining in neither crew alone.

Two or more people apart from each other come to one discovering within the same years or decades: Newton and Leibniz each form calculus in the 17th century; Darwin and Wallace each propose natural selection, their papers coming out together in 1858; and on one day in 1876 Bell's lawyer files a patent application for a telephone and Elisha Gray's lawyer a caveat for one, whether Bell's comes apart from Gray's still a dispute. Merton names such multiples the common pattern of a science and a discovering by one alone the rarer. In Merton's reading a discovering comes of a society's science and not of one self alone.

pairs.old: A lone golden shiner moves almost at random. In a school, each fish responds only to the brightness at its own place, slowing in the dark, and moves close to the fish around it; a larger school reliably goes toward shade, slowing and bunching inside it and speeding up to leave as light moves onto it, and a school below a certain size loses its tracking of the shade. Larger pigeon flocks fly significantly shorter routes than smaller flocks, and a flock's route is not simply the average of its birds' routes: each pigeon's influence on the route is in proportion to how faithfully it reproduces its own route in solo flights. In flocks of a few thousand, each bird interacts with about six or seven other birds, the same number at each distance between them. In one observing, a Photuris frontalis firefly pauses for 3.0 to 24.1 seconds, then resumes at once, synchronous with its partner. A water strider senses the ripples of prey with its front legs, and each species shares its own surface waves in courtship and in a territory.

A school's sharing goes along each fish's own seeing, from its own side, and a wave goes across the school from fish to fish.

pairs.old: In a migrating flock of young white storks, leaders fly irregular paths, searching out the rising warm air within thermals, and followers soar in more regular paths on the leaders' exploring, losing height faster between thermals and flapping more; a bird's place in the flock goes with its flying efficiency, efficient fliers going on to winter in West Africa and less efficient ones in southern Europe, a winter place foreseeable from a few minutes of flight.

In starling flocks, a field's reconstruction of each bird's place and velocity in three dimensions finds the birds' velocity changes going together over a distance growing with the flock's size, the going together having no length of its own: a change in one bird goes with each other bird's, whatever the flock's size, each bird's reach of perceiving wider than its direct interacting, and a flock's response to a disturbance stronger with it. A flock's orienting is a surface in no bird alone, each bird with its six or seven nearest and its changing going with the whole.

26 olive baboons of one troop at Mpala in Kenya wear GPS collars, 25 giving their places once a second through each day's light over the first 14 days, 16 to 25 on a day: as some baboons go out ahead in a heading, the others follow more readily as more of them go out in one heading, and with a split among them a baboon follows less readily, a deciding coming later, its authors suggest; with two headings parting under about 90 degrees a follower goes between them, and over it with one of them, more often the heading more baboons go, and with two equal parts either about equally; a baboon's rank is-not going with others following it, and the highest-ranking male is-not the one others follow most. Under about 90 degrees two headings share, each excluding its own is-not, and a heading in neither alone uncovers between them, a floating neutral, Natural Naming 5.12; over it, the following goes more with more, a troop's own heading.

A message reaches a far person through a society, each self orienting from its own side. In Travers and Milgram's letters, 296 people in Nebraska and Boston start letters toward a person working in Boston, and 64 reach him, with a mean of 5.2 people between; 3 people, each the last before the target, are in 48 percent of the chains reaching him. In Dodds, Muhamad and Watts' email chains, 61,168 senders in 166 countries, in 24,163 chains toward 18 people in 13 countries, bring 384 chains to their target in a mean of about 4 steps, a field's estimate of the median about 5 to 7 with the chains that end in its reckoning, 5 within one country and 7 across; each sender has only its own others, choosing by a place first and by a work after the third step; under 0.3 percent of senders not sending on say they find no one to send to, a lack of interest or incentive, not a difficulty, the main reason a chain ends, its authors suggest; and chains reaching their target send to hubs, a field's people with many ties, 1.6 percent against 8.2 percent in chains that end. In Kleinberg's model of a two-dimensional lattice, each holder sending the message on to its contact closest to the target finds a short path only as the lattice's long ties fall off with distance as the inverse square, its power the lattice's own dimension. A self in a society has no map of the society's ties: each sender aims from the is-not of the message's place to a person over its horizon, one parity at a time, closer or not, and a path uncovers between the senders, each with only its own others.

pairs.old: Of bighorn sheep that people move into ranges whose earlier herds are gone, under 9 percent migrate, against 65 to 100 percent in herds that stay whole; herds starting again at those ranges reach 80 percent migrating only after nearly 40 years, and moose after about 90 years; a herd's going with the spring's new growth up the slopes improving over decades, the knowledge passing from mothers and herd members to the young.

In the 1993 drought at Tarangire in Tanzania, a drought of its size coming last in 1958 to 1961, 16 of 81 elephant calves in 21 family groups of three clans die over nine months, 20 percent, against an average of 2 percent a year over the 12 years before; most of two clans' groups go out of the park, their oldest matriarchs 45 and 38 years old, and the clan going on in the park, its oldest matriarch 33 and none of it 5 years old or more in the 1958 to 1961 drought, has 11 of the 16 deaths, at least 63 percent of the deaths coming inside the park; its authors speculate that the groups going out go for food and water outside the park, perhaps with their oldest matriarchs' experience of the earlier drought. Southern resident killer whales of the North Pacific, 102 whales in some 750 hours of video over 2001 to 2009, a census over 35 years giving each whale's age: females past reproducing lead groups through salmon foraging grounds, and still more in years with few salmon, a mother leading her sons more often than her daughters. An elders' going is a society's prior same-existing, and in a hard year a self opens with it, older females leading the whales' going and, its authors speculate, the matriarchs' experience aiming the elephants'.

Mau Piailug, a master navigator from Satawal in Micronesia, navigates Hōkūleʻa from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti in 1976 with no modern instruments, the atoll of Mataiva coming after some 30 days at sea. Over two Hawaiian winters he teaches Nainoa Thompson with sand diagrams, string, shells and the feel of ocean swells at sea, and with a star compass, Hawaiian star names in a frame of the horizon; an astronomer, Will Kyselka, studies the stars' going with Thompson in the Bishop Museum's planetarium over hundreds of hours. In spring 1980 Thompson navigates Hōkūleʻa to Tahiti and back, the first Hawaiian to practise wayfinding on long ocean voyages from about the 14th century, at which voyaging between Hawaiʻi and Tahiti stops. Long voyaging by wayfinding comes again through a master navigator of Satawal: one people's going passing across to another, as a song passes between whole societies, 6.1, and along to a young self who opens with it as his prior.

Ghillar Michael Anderson, an Aboriginal Law Man, gives an account of the Euahlayi people: star maps a people learns at night go with songs of the people and the land, each star going with a feature of the land such as a waterhole, and the songs a people sings going by day along a route, routes some of Australia's highways now follow, in his account. A route goes on as a people's song, each self going along it opening with it as its prior, each star going with a place along it, in no singer alone.

pairs.old: A desert locust lives in a solitary form or a gregarious form, both in one genome. Its change goes with crowding on shrinking patches of plants, and in a laboratory with some two hours of touching a solitary locust's hind legs, as a crowd's jostling does; its serotonin in its thorax rises about threefold for less than a day; with its serotonin receptors or production blocked no change comes, and with serotonin injected and no other locusts close it comes; swarms go as billions over many square kilometres. A field's Jekyll and Hyde and a plague are its story over this: a locust in a crowd is-not stable-forming as solitary, and its genome's artifact has its next form ready, a society going.

Desert locust nymphs in an 80 cm ring arena, in Buhl and others' study as a field's report gives it: at a low crowding they mill about with no common heading; from about 25 nymphs per square metre they march together around the ring, now and then the whole band changing its heading together; and above about 75 per square metre the band goes on in one heading with no such changing; locust bands in the wild go at some 50 per square metre. A ring band's heading is a parity in no locust alone, changing and changing back together at a crowding between those two and going on at a fuller one: a society moving as its parity changes.
